newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher before CPI, jobless data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher before CPI, jobless data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Thursday ahead of a bunch of fresh economic reports.
In a market enjoying a firm tone after some overnight bargain-hunting, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 13/32 to 97-5/32 in early dealings, yielding 6.59 percent.

After a week and a half of losses, investors developed a little more taste for the cheaper securities on Wednesday after the government said wholesale prices declined in July. The government also reported a moderate retail sales gain for the month, but a smaller increase than some had come to fear.

According to a Reuters poll, economists expect that the July Consumer Price Index (CPI) due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT will be up 0.2 percent overall and up 0.2 percent excluding its more volatile food and energy components.

The Labor Department's weekly jobless claims data will be released simultaneously. Those are expected to show that new jobless claims rose to 317,000 in the week ended August 9, up from 300,000 new claims a week earlier.
Data on business inventories, also due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are expected to show a 0.6 pct June inventory rise after a 0.2 percent increase in May.

The market will have just 45 minutes to trade and register its reaction to the CPI and jobless data before getting the Federal Reserve's data on July industrial production and capacity utilization at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that U.S. industrial output rose a modest 0.2 percent in July after a 0.3 percent increase in June.
Capacity use, meanwhile, the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in that production, was forecast at 83.5 percent, unchanged from June.
Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., said he did not expect the market to make new gains on the CPI report.

"A Labor Department official suggested when the last CPI report came out that some seasonal factors that had contributed to favorable CPI readings were no longer going to be doing that in the coming months," said Stiles. "That reduces the likelihood that we're going to have a surprise number below the consensus forecast."
As for the industrial production and capacity use data, they, too, were also unlikely to "alarm" the market, he said.

The favorable July Producer Price Index (PPI) report on Wednesday allowed the market to fear the Consumer Price Index report "a little bit less," said Alan Levenson, research director at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said investors should be disinclined to sell the market at this juncture.

"I don't think they'll sell the market unless there's some big fundamental change and fundamentals haven't changed," he said. "That's the important thing. It's still a moderate growth, low inflation environment."
Alexy said the CPI could move the market.
"You have to be cautious about it but taking a look at the commodity prices and services, there are no significant price pressures there," he said.

Alexy said the market has to spend some time filling in the gap between 113 and 113-16 on the September T-bond contract. On the 30-year cash bond, "you still have to fill that gap in the yield curve in the 6.50 percent to 6.58 percent area," he said.
In early dealings, three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.17 percent. Six-month and year bill rates were each down two basis points to 5.18 percent and 5.26 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-30/32, yielding 5.91 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-11/32, yielding 6.16 percent. Ten-year notes were up 5/32 to 98-18/32, yielding 6.32 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
